body: A woman drives to work on the Monday after the worst weekend of her life. She has done her hair and put a jacket on because there is a meeting at ten and she has decided to go to it. The radio comes on with the engine and there is a man being cheerful about the traffic, and then a song telling her to lift her voice and shout for joy, and it is a good song, sung well. At the roundabout she reaches over and turns it off. She drives the last eleven minutes in silence, and she is not crying, and she is not praying either. She gets there four minutes early.

She did not turn it off because she disagreed with it. She turned it off because there was no room in it for her, and being told to shout for joy on the fourth day of something is not encouragement. It is exclusion, delivered warmly.

Roughly a third of the Psalms are laments. Not gentle reflections — complaints, addressed directly to Yahuah, sometimes angry, occasionally ending without resolution at all. Psalm 88 finishes in the dark and does not come back up.

It is worth being precise about what lament is, because the word has softened into a synonym for sadness and it is nothing of the kind. A lament is a legal shape. It addresses God by name, states the trouble without softening it, says plainly what it wants done, and very often accuses. How long. Why have you forgotten me. You have put my friends far from me. That is not a person losing faith; it is a person exercising it, because you only take a complaint to somebody you still believe is listening. That voice was collected, set to music, and sung by the congregation — which means God’s people had a public, authorised vocabulary for going to him furious.

This dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. A stretch of those frequencies is set aside for hard weeks — numbers belonging to Grief Walked, to Beyond the Trauma, to Strong Sober and The Mended Place. They are permanent allocations, and they do not have to earn a ratings book.

Keeping them is a real commitment, because nothing about them is popular. A station for the aftermath of a death, or for somebody eleven days out of a drink, delivers no audience anybody would advertise against, and on a commercial band not one of those frequencies would survive its first quarter. They are here because the songbook this whole ministry stands on is a third complaints, and a dial that only knows how to celebrate is missing most of the songbook. That is not a pastoral flourish. It is arithmetic about the material.

Somewhere along the way that material was edited out of Christian broadcasting almost entirely. Whole networks describe themselves as positive and encouraging and mean it as a promise, and you can hear why: nobody sets out to leave a family worse. But a medium committed in advance to being uplifting has committed in advance to telling one third of the human year that this is not currently the frequency for them. The person in the worst month of their life turns on the Christian station, hears that the mood is good, and quietly concludes that the trouble is with them.

So this band keeps the registers apart rather than blending them into an average. The praise and worship formats sit together in the low three hundreds, the ambient frequencies in their own places, and the stations built around a particular kind of week hold a stretch at the top of the dial — to be tuned to on purpose and left alone the rest of the year. Learn roughly where things are and you can move by feel, which a search box can never give you, because a search box requires you to name what is wrong.
None of which is an argument against joy. It is an argument about what joy costs when it is compulsory.

Be fair to the cheerful chorus first, because it is not lying. God is good, the tomb is empty, and a song that says so at volume on a Tuesday morning has lifted more people out of a low week than any amount of theology about lament. But a cheerful chorus can only do one thing for somebody who is not cheerful: it can ask them to perform. It hands them a mood to match and no words to say, and the gap between the two becomes another item on the list of ways they are failing. It cannot go with them. It can only wait, brightly, at the far end of the tunnel, shouting encouragement down it.
You cannot comfort somebody in a language that has no word for what has happened to them.

On a Sunday afternoon a woman of forty-four is ironing in a front room with the door shut, because her husband has the football on and she said she did not mind. Her son is eighteen months into a sentence and she has not told anyone at church which prison. The radio is on quietly. A song comes on that is a complaint from beginning to end — no chorus that turns it round, no bridge where everything resolves — and she irons a collar twice and then stands there with the iron up. When it finishes she puts it back to the start and listens again. Then she does the rest of the basket, and at no point in that hour does she feel better in the way that word is normally used.

Something was given to her that afternoon, and it was not comfort. It was permission and a vocabulary in the same three and a half minutes: this is sayable, out loud, to God, and here are the words for it.

The honest cost of giving grief a frequency is that a frequency can become a place to live. Music that agrees with you is powerful, and it does not always want to let you go. A person can tune to the station that matches the inside of their head and stay there for a year, taking the fact that it never contradicts them as evidence that nothing can. Anybody who has watched a friend curate their own sadness knows exactly what that looks like.

Which is why lament is a frequency on this dial and not the dial itself. The Psalter does not end at 88 — the same collection carries the complaint and the song after the sea, bound together, sung by the same congregation. That is the design being copied here. Grief gets a real number, permanently, so nobody has to pretend on the way in. And it sits on a band where praise is a few frequencies away, playing whether or not you are ready, for the morning some months off when you find that you are.

So the claim is simply this: a station that cannot say how long is not more faithful than the Psalms, it is less. Lament is not the failure of worship, nor the waiting room outside it. It is a third of the songbook, sung to God by his own people at his own invitation, and a dial built to carry the Word has to carry that part of it too.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you are in one of these weeks now, begin at HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise. It is ambient worship, which in practice means unhurried, wordless in long stretches, and requiring nothing of you: it will not ask you to lift your hands, will not tell you how to feel about the morning, and will not brighten up when you walk into the room. Paul and Silas sang at midnight with their feet in the stocks, and nothing in that account suggests it was upbeat. Put it on at the hour when the house has gone quiet and the quiet has got loud, and let it hold the room while you lie there not sleeping. It will not fix Monday. It will keep you company in a way a cheerful station structurally cannot.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than advice, since advice is the last thing anybody in a bad month needs more of. You do not have to feel better to turn a radio on, and you do not have to arrive at a station with your face arranged. Put HM 314.40 on tonight and leave it running while you do something ordinary. A third of the songbook has been waiting for you, and none of it requires you to shout for joy first.
